title: Kernelized Activation Steering

paper.title: Kernelized Activation Steering
paper.abstract:
Abstract Activation steering provides a simple, training-free mechanism for controlling attributes of generative models such as sentiment, style, and helpfulness. However, standard approaches such as Difference-in-Means apply a single input-independent steering vector across all activations, limiting expressivity and ignoring the local geometry of the activation space.
We propose Kernelized Activation Steering (KAS), a unifying framework that lifts activation steering into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. KAS formulates steering as an optimization problem expressed purely via kernel evaluations, yielding an implicit, activation-dependent steering score without constructing explicit feature maps.
Unlike DiM, KAS induces locally adaptive steering: each activation is modified according to its relative position with respect to source and target reference sets, producing a nonlinear steering field over the representation space. Importantly, DiM is recovered as a special case under a linear kernel, while richer kernels enable geometry-aware interventions.
Across standard activation steering tasks, including jailbreaking LLMs and image style control, KAS outperforms or is on par with the existing methods.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) are now known to encode rich semantic concepts such as sentiment, refusal, truthfulness, persona as identifiable structures in their internal representations ( Tigges et al., 2024 ; Marks and Tegmark, 2024 ; Arditi et al., 2024 ) . A central problem in alignment and controllability is to manipulate these structures at inference time , in order to alter behaviour without the cost or fragility of full fine-tuning. Activation steering ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Arditi et al., 2024 ) has emerged as a particularly practical instrument for this purpose: it modifies a single layer’s activations using a precomputed direction and requires no parameter updates. The dominant instantiation of this idea is Difference-in-Means (DiM) ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Turner et al., 2023 ; Arditi et al., 2024 ) , which estimates the steering direction as the difference between mean activations on a source dataset (behaviour to suppress) and a target dataset (behaviour to elicit). DiM derives both its appeal and its limitations from the linear representation hypothesis (LRH) ( Park et al., 2024 ; Mikolov et al., 2013 ; Arora et al., 2018 ; Elhage et al., 2022 ) — the assumption that high-level concepts are encoded as linear directions in activation space. While the LRH has proven surprisingly robust for many tasks, mounting evidence highlights pervasive polysemanticity and curved structure in transformer representations ( Engels et al., 2025 ; Elhage et al., 2022 ) , where features cluster along nonlinear manifolds that no single global translation can faithfully capture. As a consequence, DiM-style interventions can be either ineffective on out-of-distribution activations or destructive of unrelated capabilities once the steering coefficient is increased to compensate. We propose Kernelized Activation Steering (KAS) , a framework that retains the simplicity of DiM while relaxing its linear constraint via the kernel trick. We lift activations into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) ℋ \mathcal{H} , define the feature-space steering direction as the lifted DiM vector, and derive an implicit steering score that depends on the input only through kernel evaluations against the reference sets. Steering then proceeds by gradient ascent on this score with a proximal regulariser that bounds deviation from the original activation. Because kernel gradients themselves depend on the current activation, the resulting update is locally adaptive: KAS attracts activations toward target reference points and repels them from source reference points, producing a nonlinear steering field (see Figure 1 ). Crucially, KAS recovers DiM exactly under a linear kernel, situating it as a strict generalization rather than an alternative. Overall, our contributions are threefold: 1. A nonlinear generalization of activation steering. We formulate activation steering as optimization in an RKHS and derive an implicit steering score that requires only kernel evaluations between the input and the source/target reference sets (§ 4 ). Furthermore, DiM is recovered exactly under the linear kernel (Remark 4.1 ), unifying classical kernel methods with modern activation-level interventions. 2. A theoretical bridge between activation steering and kernel two-sample test. We show that the KAS score is the empirical witness function associated with maximum mean discrepancy, connecting activation steering to kernel two-sample testing and explaining how characteristic kernels can detect distributional differences that linear mean-based steering misses. 3. A locally adaptive RBF instantiation. We instantiate the framework with the Gaussian RBF kernel, yielding a closed-form, activation-dependent gradient update (§ 4.3 ). We evaluate KAS on jailbreak steering across three instruction-tuned LLMs, CAA-style behavioral steering, and text-to-image style control. KAS improves jailbreak attack success over ActAdd on Gemma and Qwen while matching it on Llama, achieves the strongest effects on four CAA behaviors with non-null steering responses, and improves style induction over Mean-AcT across most tested intervention strengths while preserving prompt alignment. Additional ablations examine kernel approximation and steering from a single contrastive pair (§ 5 ). Figure 1: An illustrative comparison between standard Difference-in-Means (DiM) and Kernelized Activation Steering (KAS). Source activations (orange) lie between two target modes (blue). (a) DiM applies a single global translation 𝒗 = μ B − μ A \bm{v}=\mu_{B}-\mu_{A} , sending every activation into the saddle between the modes, a region with no semantic content under either target behaviour. No choice of steering strength α \alpha recovers the modes. (b) Kernelized activation steering (KAS) produces a data-adaptive vector field that routes each activation to its nearest mode.

sections.heading: 2 Preliminaries
sections.text: Notation. We write [ n ] := { 1 , … , n } [n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\} for any positive integer n n . For a decoder-only transformer ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , we denote by 𝒙 ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ d \bm{x}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} the residual-stream activation at layer ℓ ∈ [ L ] \ell\in[L] for a given input prompt. Activation Steering via Difference-in-Means. Activation steering modifies a model’s behaviour at inference time by directly intervening on internal activations, without updating parameters. Given a contrastive pair of prompt sets — a source set A A exhibiting behaviour to suppress and a target set B B exhibiting behaviour to elicit — the difference-in-means (DiM) method ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Turner et al., 2023 ; Arditi et al., 2024 ; Venhoff et al., 2025 ) extracts a steering vector by contrasting their mean activations: 𝒗 = 1 n B ​ ∑ j ∈ [ n B ] 𝒃 j − 1 n A ​ ∑ i ∈ [ n A ] 𝒂 i , \bm{v}=\frac{1}{n_{B}}\sum_{j\in[n_{B}]}\bm{b}_{j}-\frac{1}{n_{A}}\sum_{i\in[n_{A}]}\bm{a}_{i}, (1) where { 𝒂 i } i ∈ [ n A ] \{\bm{a}_{i}\}_{i\in[n_{A}]} and { 𝒃 j } j ∈ [ n B ] \{\bm{b}_{j}\}_{j\in[n_{B}]} are the layer- ℓ ∗ \ell^{*} activations of prompts in A A and B B . At inference, an incoming activation 𝒙 \bm{x} is steered by the additive update 𝒙 ← 𝒙 + α ​ 𝒗 , \bm{x}\;\leftarrow\;\bm{x}+\alpha\,\bm{v}, (2) where α ∈ ℝ \alpha\in\mathbb{R} controls the intervention strength. The intervention layer ℓ ∗ \ell^{*} is typically chosen on a held-out validation set ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) . A defining property of DiM is that the steering direction 𝒗 \bm{v} is global and input-independent : every activation receives the same translation, regardless of where it sits in representation space. Our work generalises this construction to allow activation-dependent steering through a kernelised formulation. Kernel Methods and Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces. A function k : 𝒳 × 𝒳 → ℝ k:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} is a positive semi-definite (PSD) kernel if, for any finite set { 𝒙 i } i = 1 n ⊂ 𝒳 \{\bm{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\subset\mathcal{X} , the Gram matrix K ∈ ℝ n × n K\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} with entries K i ​ j = k ⁡ ( 𝒙 i , 𝒙 j ) K_{ij}=k(\bm{x}_{i},\bm{x}_{j}) is positive semi-definite. By the Moore–Aronszajn theorem ( Aronszajn, 1950 ; Berlinet and Thomas-Agnan, 2004 ) , every PSD kernel uniquely defines a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) ℋ \mathcal{H} together with a feature map φ : 𝒳 → ℋ \varphi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{H} satisfying k ⁡ ( 𝒙 , 𝒚 ) = ⟨ φ ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) , φ ⁡ ( 𝒚 ) ⟩ ℋ k(\bm{x},\bm{y})\;=\;\langle\varphi(\bm{x}),\,\varphi(\bm{y})\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} for all 𝒙 , 𝒚 ∈ 𝒳 \bm{x},\bm{y}\in\mathcal{X} . The kernel trick states that any algorithm expressible solely through inner products in ℋ \mathcal{H} can be implemented using only kernel evaluations on 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , without materializing φ \varphi . This is what enables us to operate in a high- or infinite-dimensional feature space at the cost of 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ) \mathcal{O}(n) kernel evaluations per query ( Schölkopf and Smola, 2002 ; Hofmann et al., 2008 ) . Kernel methods are usually favorable as it is believed that most nonlinear systems behave approximately linearly in higher, possibly infinite-dimensional feature spaces ( Cover, 1965 ; Bouvrie and Hamzi, 2017 ) .

sections.heading: 3 Related Work
sections.text: Activation-level interventions on language models have been studied under several names, including activation addition ( Turner et al., 2023 ) , representation engineering ( Zou et al., 2023a ) , contrastive activation addition ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) , and inference-time intervention ( Li et al., 2023 ) . Most of these methods extract a single steering direction per concept via difference-in-means, linear probing, or PCA on contrastive activations ( Alain and Bengio, 2016 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Zou et al., 2023a ; Teo et al., 2025 ) . A separate line of work uses sparse autoencoders to identify steerable features ( Templeton et al., 2024 ; O’Brien et al., 2024 ; Bayat et al., 2025 ; Kantamneni et al., 2025 ; Xie, 2025 ) . However, most of these approaches apply a fixed translation in activation space and thus inherit the limitations of input-independent steering. To address this issue, there is a growing body of work dedicated to designing input-dependent steering mechanisms. K-steer ( Oozeer et al., 2025 ) trains a nonlinear attribute classifier on hidden activations and computes steering directions via gradients of that classifier while SAS ( Bayat et al., 2025 ) relies on pretrained SAEs as nonlinear feature extractors. Another line of research models activation steering via Optimal Transport ( Rodriguez et al., 2024 ) through which a numerous input-dependent affine ( Singh et al., 2024 ) and nonlinear ( Abdullaev et al., 2026 ) steering methods have been proposed. Perhaps the closest to our method is Curveball steering ( Raval et al., 2026 ) , which uses kernel PCA for nonlinear dimensionality reduction and perform steering in the reduced space while ( Saillenfest and Lemberger, 2025 ) employs a similar technique for concept erasure problem ( Ravfogel et al., 2020 ; Belrose et al., 2023 ; Chowdhury et al., 2025 ) . More broadly, kernel methods have been used for distribution matching in generative modeling ( Li et al., 2015 ) , particle-based variational inference ( Liu and Wang, 2016 ) , and mode seeking in diffusion-based image restoration ( Hu et al., 2025 ) , providing related distributional perspectives. Our training-free framework, Kernelized Activation Steering (KAS), instead derives an activation-dependent intervention from an interpretable, kernel-based optimization objective and recovers DiM exactly as a special case under a linear kernel, along with a relation to hypothesis testing techniques ( Gretton et al., 2012 ; Muandet et al., 2017 ) providing a complementary theoretical lens for activation steering design.

sections.heading: 4 Kernelized Activation Steering
sections.text: Let { 𝒂 i } i ∈ [ n A ] \{\bm{a}_{i}\}_{i\in[n_{A}]} and { 𝒃 j } j ∈ [ n B ] \{\bm{b}_{j}\}_{j\in[n_{B}]} denote the layer- ℓ ∗ \ell^{*} activations of prompts drawn from a source set A A and target set B B , respectively. The DiM steering vector ( 1 ) is effective when A A and B B are well separated by a linear hyperplane in activation space, but totally disregards local structures of the activation distributions and possible nonlinearities in decision boundary. To approach these issues properly, we shall derive DiM activation steering as a special case of a more general, principled operation in the following section.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate KAS across three settings that exercise different aspects of activation steering: (i) jailbreak steering on instruction-tuned LLMs, which trades off attack success against general-capability retention; (ii) CAA-style contrastive steering on multiple-choice question answering, which isolates targeted behavioral control on a fixed answer-token position; and (iii) text-to-image style control on a diffusion model, which probes whether KAS generalizes beyond language modeling. Sections 5.4 and 5.5 examine kernel approximation and data efficiency, respectively. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA H100 96GB GPU.

sections.text: Setup. We adopt the contrastive multiple-choice setup of CAA ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Each pair shares a question and differs only in the appended answer: the positive example selects the behavior-consistent option and the negative example selects the opposite option. Activations are collected at the answer-token position. For each behavior, we retain 50 held-out test questions, remove duplicates and test-set overlaps from the generation pool, sample 50 validation questions, and use the remaining examples as references. Layer and strength are selected by maximizing behavior-consistent answer probability on the validation set; the selected configuration is then evaluated on the test set. Experiments use Gemma-2-9B-IT at layer 22 or 23. We consider no system prompt, a positive system prompt encouraging the behavior, and a negative system prompt discouraging it. sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We examine the effect of approximating the KAS kernel using the Nyström method ( Williams and Seeger, 2000 ) with 64 landmarks sampled without replacement from the reference sets. Appendix A.4 derives the approximate score and steering update. We compare this variant, denoted Nyström-KAS, with exact KAS under the reference, validation, and test protocols of Sections 5.1 and 5.2 . Each variant uses its own validation-selected layer and strength; the comparison therefore measures performance after selection rather than approximation error at a fixed intervention. Nyström results report mean and standard deviation over three landmark-sampling seeds.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Table 3 shows that the approximation reduces jailbreak ASR on all three models, with slightly lower Alpaca perplexity. In contrast, Table 4 shows that the approximation improves AI Coordination and Corrigibility, while exact KAS achieves higher probabilities on Hallucination and Myopic Reward. Both variants exhibit near-null effects on Survival Instinct and Sycophancy. Thus, the effect of kernel approximation depends on the task; these results do not establish a uniform substitute for exact kernel evaluation or quantify computational savings.

sections.heading: 5.5 Ablation: Jailbreaking from a Single Contrastive Pair
sections.text: Figure 5: Single-pair jailbreak steering across three instruction-tuned models. Box plots report attack success rate (ASR), Pile perplexity, and Alpaca perplexity over ten randomly sampled harmful–harmless contrastive prompt pairs. Steering is applied at layer 22 for Gemma-2-9B-IT , layer 12 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct , and layer 18 for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct . KAS is evaluated with one gradient step and ten gradient steps using the step sizes shown on the x-axis, and is compared against ActAdd. We further evaluate whether jailbreak steering can be induced from an extremely limited contrastive set. In this ablation, each steering direction is extracted from only one harmful–harmless prompt pair. We repeat this procedure over ten randomly sampled contrastive pairs and evaluate using the same protocol as in Section 5.1 . To quantify the extent each steering method maintains general capabilities of the model, we also measure perplexity on the Pile ( Gao et al., 2020 ) and Alpaca ( Taori et al., 2023 ) datasets. This setting provides a stress test for data efficiency: a successful method must be able to recover a useful behavioral direction from a minimal number of contrastive examples while avoiding severe degradation of generation quality. Figure 5 visualizes the distribution of one-shot jailbreak steering performance across ten randomly sampled contrastive prompt pairs. The main trend is that KAS preserves general utility substantially better than ActAdd while remaining competitive in ASR. On Gemma-2-9B-IT , KAS achieves ASR comparable to ActAdd, with both one-step and ten-step variants attaining similar mean ASR while reducing Pile and Alpaca perplexity. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct , KAS remains comparable to ActAdd in ASR, but yields markedly lower perplexity on both utility corpora. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct , ActAdd obtains the highest ASR, yet KAS substantially reduces perplexity. Overall, KAS remains effective under this severe data constraint while improving generation stability relative to a global linear intervention.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced Kernelized Activation Steering (KAS), a unifying framework that recasts activation steering as optimization in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. By expressing the steering objective entirely through kernel evaluations, KAS produces an implicit, activation-dependent steering field that is locally adaptive to the geometry of the representation manifold, while strictly generalizing the classical Difference-in-Means construction, which is recovered exactly under a linear kernel. We view KAS as a step toward a more principled, geometry-aware approach to inference-time control of generative models, and an opening for further work on kernel design and adaptive layer selection. A limitation of KAS is that the intervention applies a uniform number of gradient ascent steps to every token, which is computationally wasteful for tokens already close to the target manifold and potentially insufficient for harder ones. A token-adaptive compute schedule would likely improve both efficiency and stability. While RBF is shown to be a reliable default kernel choice, a principled method to choose the kernel function given a specific steering task or requirements remains a promising open direction to explore in future work.

sections.heading: B.3 CAA-style Multiple-choice Steering Details
sections.text: For CAA-style evaluation, each contrastive pair shares the same multiple-choice question but differs only in the appended answer option. Positive examples append the behavior-consistent answer, whereas negative examples append the opposite answer. Activations are extracted at the answer-token position. We evaluate on 50 held-out questions per behavior and report the average probability assigned to the behavior-consistent option. Dataset sourcing. The behavioral datasets span several alignment-relevant attributes: AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, and Sycophancy. Except for Hallucination, these datasets are drawn primarily from Anthropic’s Advanced AI Risk human-written evaluations [ 37 ] . The Hallucination dataset is constructed separately from GPT-4-generated contrastive multiple-choice questions. System-prompt conditions. We evaluate three prompting conditions: no system prompt, a positive system prompt that encourages the target behavior, and a negative system prompt that discourages the target behavior. These settings allow us to test whether steering remains effective when the prompt context is neutral, aligned with the target concept, or opposed to it. Hyperparameter selection. For the CAA-style multiple-choice experiments, all methods are evaluated on Gemma-2-9B-IT . We sweep the intervention layer over 22, 23 and select the best configuration according to the average token probability assigned to the behavior-consistent answer on the validation set. We then evaluate the selected configuration on the disjoint test set. For both ActAdd and KAS, we sweep the steering strength η \eta over 0.01, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 2.0, 2.25, 2.5, 2.75, 3.0, 3.25, 3.5, 3.75, 4.0, 4.25, 4.5, 4.75, 5.0, 7.5, 10.0, 12.5, 15.0, 17.5, 20.0, 22.5, 25.0, 27.5, 30.0, 32.5, 35.0, 37.5, 40.0, 42.5, 45.0, 47.5, 50.0, 55.0, 60.0, 62.5, 65.0, 70.0, 75.0, 80.0, 85.0, 87.5, 90.0, 95.0, 100.0, 112.5, 125.0, 137.5, 150.0, 162.5, 175.0, 187.5, 200.0, 225.0, 250.0, 275.0, 300.0, 325.0, 350.0, 355.0, 360.0, 365.0, 370.0, 375.0, 380.0, 385.0, 390.0, 395.0, 400.0, 405.0, 410.0, 420.0, 425.0, 430.0, 435.0, 440.0, 445.0, 450.0, 500.0, 625.0, 750.0.

sections.heading: Appendix D Broader Impacts
sections.text: Kernelized Activation Steering (KAS) provides a training-free mechanism for modifying model behavior at inference time. This has potential positive applications in controllability, safety evaluation, and model debugging. By enabling behavior-specific interventions without updating model parameters, KAS may help practitioners study how target attributes are represented in internal activations, evaluate the robustness of safety mechanisms, and develop more fine-grained tools for aligning model outputs with user- or deployment-specific requirements. More broadly, geometry-aware steering methods may contribute to more interpretable and adaptive forms of model control than global linear interventions. At the same time, activation steering is inherently dual-use. The same mechanisms that can suppress undesirable behavior or improve controllability can also be used to elicit harmful behavior, bypass refusal mechanisms, or manipulate model responses in unintended ways. This concern is particularly relevant for our jailbreak experiments. These experiments are included to measure controllability and expose weaknesses in current alignment mechanisms, not to encourage misuse. We therefore view KAS as both a potential safety tool and a method that should be handled with care. To reduce misuse risk, we emphasize the need for appropriate safeguards, clear documentation of intended use, and accountability in deployment. Practitioners applying KAS beyond controlled research settings should perform downstream safety evaluations before release. We further encourage continued ethical review of inference-time steering methods to ensure that their use remains aligned with safety, transparency, and responsible deployment practices.

sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract and introduction state the main contributions of KAS: a training-free, kernelized generalization of activation steering, a closed-form RBF instantiation, and a theoretical connection to DiM. The empirical claims are limited to the evaluated jailbreak, CAA-style multiple-choice, and image style-control settings. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proofs for the main theorems in Appendix A.1 . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper specifies the evaluated models, datasets, baselines, metrics, intervention layers, steering settings, and hyperparameter search procedures. Additional implementation details and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix B . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution.
